lead: A car in 1960 used electricity mainly for starting, ignition and lamps. A car today uses electronics for engine control, braking, steering, comfort and safety. This chapter traces that change as a cause-and-effect chain: bigger electrical loads demanded better charging; emission and safety laws demanded precise control; precise control demanded sensors, actuators and networks. The chain explains why the 12 V battery, alternator, ECU and CAN bus sit together in one system. It also prepares you to study batteries, starting and charging in the rest of this unit.
prereq: You need: basic DC circuits from first-year physics (voltage, current, resistance and power); for the battery itself see Chapter 1.4.

sections.h3: From hand crank to a regulated 12 V bus

blocks.text: Early petrol cars were started by hand. The driver turned a crank, which rotated the crankshaft until the engine fired. A magneto, a small generator driven by the engine, made the high-voltage spark. The only electrical load was ignition, so a battery was optional. Hand cranking was dangerous: a mis-timed kick could break a wrist.

Battery-coil ignition changed the pattern. A battery supplied current to an ignition coil, the coil stepped voltage up, and a distributor sent the pulse to each spark plug. In 1912 the electric self-starter (on the Cadillac, designed by Charles Kettering) made starting an electric motor job, so the car needed a rechargeable battery, and a belt-driven dynamo charged it. The system voltage was 6 V at first. As lamps, wipers and radios were added, current grew and the voltage drop in the cables became a problem. From the mid-1950s car makers moved to 12 V systems: the battery is nominally 12 V (about 12.6 V at rest) and the charging system holds the bus near 14 V while the engine runs.

The dynamo had a commutator and brushes, and its output was limited at low engine speed. From 1960 the alternator began to replace it: a rotating field winding induces three-phase AC in stationary stator coils, and a diode bridge rectifies the AC to DC. It charges even at idle. The voltage regulator holds the bus near 14 V by adjusting field current. See Chapter 1.6 and Chapter 1.7 for the circuits and curves.

sections.h3: Emission laws pull electronics into the engine

blocks.text: From the 1970s, first the United States and Japan and then Europe limited carbon monoxide (CO), hydrocarbons (HC) and nitrogen oxides (NOx) from petrol engines. The European steps are numbered Euro I to Euro 6, and India adopted matching Bharat Stage (BS) norms a few years behind each Euro step, then jumped from BS IV straight to BS VI in April 2020. The table gives the years; the limits and test cycles themselves come with the emission norms in electronic engine control. Here the point is cause and effect: a carburettor meters fuel by mechanical jets and cannot hold a precise air-fuel ratio as speed, load and temperature change. A three-way catalytic converter needs the ratio held near the chemically correct value, so mechanical fuelling was not enough.

Electronic fuel injection (EFI) replaced the carburettor on new petrol cars. An electronic control unit (ECU) reads sensors: air flow or manifold pressure, crank position, throttle position, coolant temperature and exhaust oxygen. It calculates injector pulse width and ignition timing, then drives injectors and the ignition coil. The same ECU can diagnose faults and store codes. Sensors and actuators, and fuel and spark control, are later topics of this subject. Electronic ignition first removed contact points, which wore and needed gap setting. A reluctor or Hall sensor triggered a transistor, giving a stable spark.

The result is a feedback loop. The oxygen sensor measures leftover oxygen in exhaust; the ECU trims fuel until the mixture returns to target. This loop cuts emissions and holds fuel economy. It also makes the engine dependent on electrical power and signal quality.

sections.h3: Networks, assistance and the system map

blocks.text: As ECUs multiplied, separate wires for every signal became heavy and hard to diagnose. A data bus lets many controllers share a pair of wires. CAN (Controller Area Network), developed by Bosch in the 1980s and first used in a production car in 1991, is the common bus in cars; it carries short messages with identifiers and error checks. CAN frames and protocols come with in-vehicle networks. The bus joins engine, transmission, brake and body controllers. On-board diagnostics (OBD-II) at first allowed several protocols; CAN became the required one for new cars in the United States from the 2008 model year.

Safety systems followed the same path. Anti-lock braking, electronic stability program and airbags need fast sensing and actuation; adaptive cruise control and automatic emergency braking add radar, camera and fusion. These are advanced driver assistance systems (ADAS), covered with vehicle motion control and safety. Electric and hybrid traction adds a high-voltage battery and inverter beside the 12 V bus; the separation and safety devices are in Chapter 1.11.

One system map keeps the mechanical and electrical sides together. The engine block holds the cylinders; the cylinder head holds valves and camshaft; pistons connect through connecting rods to the crankshaft. The four-stroke cycle needs spark and fuel at the right instant, so crank and cam sensors feed the ECU. The drivetrain takes torque through the transmission, drive shaft and differential to the wheels. Suspension, brakes and steering are controlled or assisted electrically. None of these parts is redesigned here; the electrical system serves them.

figure.caption: From hand cranking to networked control. Growing loads pushed the early steps (12 V, the alternator); emission laws pushed engine electronics; safety and comfort pushed networks and driver assistance.

spec.aria: A timeline from 1912 to the 2010s: electric self-starter, 6 V to 12 V, the alternator in 1960, electronic ignition, fuel injection and ECU, CAN bus in 1991, ADAS and 48 V. Bands below show the pressure behind each group of steps.

examples.question: A 1970 car has a 35 A dynamo; a 2020 car has a 120 A alternator. Both are regulated at 14.0 V. Compare the maximum electrical power available.
steps: Use P = V × I, where P is power in watts, V is the regulated bus voltage in volts, and I is current in amperes.
Increase = P₂ − P₁ = 1680 W − 490 W = 1190 W.
examples.answer: The 2020 alternator can supply 1680 W against 490 W, an increase of 1190 W, about 3.4 times the 1970 value.

examples.question: A car of the 1950s has 300 W of lamps and accessories. The feed cable and its connections have a resistance of 0.01 Ω. Compare a 6 V system with a 12 V system: find the current, the voltage drop in the cable, the drop as a percentage of the system voltage, and the power lost in the cable.
steps: 6 V system: I = P ÷ V = 300 W ÷ 6 V = 50 A.
Cable drop: ΔV = I × R = 50 A × 0.01 Ω = 0.5 V, which is 0.5 ÷ 6 × 100 = 8.3 % of the supply.
Doubling the voltage halved the current, halved the drop in volts, cut the percentage drop to a quarter and cut the cable loss to a quarter (loss goes with I²).
examples.answer: At 6 V the load draws 50 A, drops 0.5 V (8.3 %) and wastes 25 W in the cable; at 12 V it draws 25 A, drops 0.25 V (2.1 %) and wastes 6.25 W, a quarter of the loss.

traps: The evolution was driven by emission limits, safety rules and customer loads, not by a wish for more gadgets.
A dynamo and an alternator are not the same: the dynamo uses a commutator to make DC; the alternator makes AC and rectifies it with diodes.
12 V is a nominal battery voltage; a charging system runs near 14.0 V. Do not use 12 V when a question gives the regulated bus.
Bharat Stage and Euro norms are matching regulatory steps, not two different physical processes; India skipped the Euro V equivalent and went from BS IV to BS VI.
Power is volts times amperes; energy is power times time. A 120 A alternator does not store 120 Ah; the battery rating is separate.

quiz.q: Name the device that replaced the dynamo and give one advantage.
quiz.a: Alternator. It rectifies three-phase AC with diodes and can charge at idle.

quiz.q: What does CAN stand for, and what does it replace?
quiz.a: Controller Area Network. It replaces many separate signal wires with a shared data bus.

quiz.q: Why did the car electrical system move from 6 V to 12 V?
quiz.a: More loads meant more current. For the same power, doubling voltage halves current, so cables can be thinner and voltage drop is lower.

quiz.q: Why did electronic ignition replace contact points?
quiz.a: Contact points wear, need gap setting and can bounce. An electronic trigger gives stable timing and needs less maintenance.

quiz.q: A 14.0 V bus supplies a 60 W lamp and a 30 W ECU. Find the total current.
quiz.a: Total power = 60 W + 30 W = 90 W. I = P/V = 90 W ÷ 14.0 V = 6.43 A.

quiz.q: Explain the cause-and-effect link from Bharat Stage norms to EFI.
quiz.a: Tighter limits need a catalytic converter working near the correct air-fuel ratio. A carburettor cannot hold that ratio precisely. An oxygen sensor gives feedback, and the ECU adjusts injector pulse width, so EFI is needed.

quiz.q: A 120 A alternator at 14.0 V feeds a 900 W load. Find the current left for charging.
quiz.a: Load current = 900 W ÷ 14.0 V = 64.3 A. Spare current = 120 A − 64.3 A = 55.7 A.

quiz.q: A car has a 12 V battery, a 14.0 V alternator, a CAN bus and ADAS. Explain why one loose ground wire can disturb several systems.
quiz.a: The ground is the return path and the voltage reference. A high-resistance ground shifts sensor voltages, causes bus errors and makes actuators misread commands. Shared references couple the fault across ECUs.

beyond: Not for the exam. In industry, the 12 V bus is being supplemented by 48 V mild-hybrid systems to cut cable current and recover braking energy. Zonal architectures replace many ECUs with a few domain controllers and Ethernet backbones. Functional safety standard ISO 26262 and coding rules such as MISRA shape software. Search next for automotive Ethernet, zonal E/E architecture, AUTOSAR and ISO 26262.
